production-function-s3.title: Copperline Print Shop adds workers
production-function-s3.html: Copperline Print Shop owns two printing presses and cannot buy more this month. With one worker, that worker sets up jobs, runs the presses and packs orders. With two or three workers, one sets up jobs while the others run the presses, and output per worker climbs. By the sixth worker, people are waiting in line for a free press, and each new worker adds less output than the one before. (An invented business, for practice.)

long-run-costs-s3.title: Sunmere Solar grows its factory
long-run-costs-s3.html: Sunmere Solar doubles every input it uses: workers, assembly lines, floor space and machines. Its weekly output of solar panels rises from 1,000 to 2,500. Years later, at a much larger size, it doubles every input again, and weekly output rises from 4,000 to 7,000. Input prices stay the same throughout. (An invented business, for practice.)

types-of-profit-s1.title: Rosa Quill's bakery: explicit and implicit costs
types-of-profit-s1.html: Rosa Quill quit a job that paid $45,000 a year to run her own bakery, Quill and Crumb. She also put $50,000 of her savings into the business; in a savings account that money would have earned $2,000 a year in interest. Last year the bakery took in $180,000 in revenue and paid $30,000 in rent, $50,000 for ingredients and $40,000 in wages to two employees. (An invented business, for practice.)

firm-decisions-s3.title: Yoga studios after a fall in demand
firm-decisions-s3.html: A city has dozens of small yoga studios, each charging the going price for a class. After a large gym chain opens nearby with free classes for members, demand for studio classes falls and the market price drops. At the new price, a typical studio covers its variable costs (instructors, heating) but not its rent, so it makes an economic loss. (An invented situation, for practice.)

perfect-competition-s3.title: Sea salt harvesters on the Tarrow coast
perfect-competition-s3.html: Hundreds of small harvesters gather sea salt along the Tarrow coast. Buyers see the salt from one harvester as the same as any other's, and prices are posted at a daily market, so every buyer knows the going price. Anyone can rent a stretch of shore and start harvesting, and a harvester can stop and sell her equipment at any time. (An invented market, for practice.)

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal product of the fourth picker, in baskets per day?

mistakes.why: That is the average product of four pickers (56 / 4 = 14). Marginal product is the change in total product from the third to the fourth picker.
That is the total product with four pickers. Marginal product is the extra output the fourth picker adds: subtract 45 from 56.

items.q: Use the table. What is the average product when the farm has five pickers, in baskets per picker?

mistakes.why: That is the marginal product of the fifth picker (62 - 56 = 6). Average product is total product divided by the number of pickers.
That is total product. Divide it by the five pickers to get output per picker.

mistakes.why: That is the change in total product for both workers together. Divide by the change in labor (2 workers).
That is the average product of 12 workers. Marginal product uses the change in output and the change in labor.

items.q: Make the explanation specific: a restaurant adds cooks to a kitchen with one stove. Fill in each blank.

specific.frame: Because the ___ is fixed, each added cook has ___ of it to use, so the marginal product of each cook ___.

input.label: The fixed input
options: stove
number of cooks

why.1: The number of cooks is what changes; the stove is the fixed input.

share.label: How much each cook has
options: less
more

why.1: More cooks share one stove, so each has less of it, not more.

mp.label: Marginal product
options: falls
rises

why.1: Once cooks crowd the stove, each added cook adds less than the one before.

specific.model: Because the stove is fixed, each added cook has less of it to use, so the marginal product of each added cook falls: diminishing marginal returns.

items.q: A tutoring center's five tutors have an average product of 20 sessions a week. A sixth tutor would add 14 sessions. What would the average product of six tutors be, in sessions per tutor?

mistakes.why: That averages 20 and 14 as if they were two equal groups. Find total product first: 5 x 20 + 14 = 114 sessions.
That is the sixth tutor's marginal product, not the average for all six.

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal cost of a candle when output rises from 30 to 40 candles a day, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is the change in total cost for all 10 candles. Marginal cost is per unit: divide $70 by the change in output, 10 candles.

mistakes.why: That is average total cost (360 / 40). Subtract the fixed cost first: variable cost is 360 - 100 = 260.

mistakes.why: That also subtracts implicit costs; that is economic profit. An accountant subtracts only the explicit costs.

mistakes.why: That is accounting profit. Economic profit also subtracts the implicit costs of $47,000.

items.q: Make the explanation specific: a firm shows an accounting profit of $30,000, and its owner gave up a $40,000 job to run it. Fill in each blank.

specific.frame: Economic profit also subtracts ___ costs, so because the owner's ___ is larger than the accounting profit, economic profit is ___ zero.

kind.label: Which costs
options: implicit
explicit

why.1: Accounting profit already subtracts explicit costs; economic profit adds the implicit ones.

what.label: What is larger
options: forgone salary
rent payment

why.1: Rent is an explicit cost, already in accounting profit; the forgone salary is the implicit cost.

sign.label: Economic profit
options: less than
greater than

why.1: 30,000 - 40,000 = -10,000, which is less than zero: an economic loss.

specific.model: Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, so because the owner's forgone salary of $40,000 is larger than the $30,000 accounting profit, economic profit is less than zero: an economic loss of $10,000.

items.q: A firm's accounting profit is $40,000 and its economic profit is $10,000. What are its implicit costs, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That adds the two profits. Implicit costs are the gap between them: 40,000 - 10,000.
That is the economic profit, not the implicit costs.

items.q: What is normal profit?

Any profit above the owner's explicit costs

A loss small enough that the firm keeps going

items.q: Make the explanation specific: why does a firm produce where MR = MC? Fill in each blank.

specific.frame: Below that output each unit adds ___ to revenue than to cost, so producing it raises profit; above it each unit adds ___ to cost than to revenue, so profit ___.

below.label: Below the output

less

above.label: Above the output
options: more
less

why.1: Above it, MC is greater than MR, so units add more to cost.

profit.label: Profit
options: falls
rises

why.1: A unit that adds more to cost than to revenue lowers profit.

specific.model: Below that output each unit adds more to revenue than to cost, so producing it raises profit; above it each unit adds more to cost than to revenue, so profit falls. Profit is greatest where MR = MC because no unit is left that would raise it.
